name: Ben Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive for a pallet network depot. In the afternoon I collect pallets from small firms around the area, a printer, a bathroom supplier, a brewery, and bring them back to the depot, and some nights I do the run to the national hub. It's a rigid with a tail lift, so I'm on and off with the pump truck all day. I like that every day is a puzzle, and I hate the brewery's yard, which is on a hill.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at the depot, and what else do you do?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fifteen months, so I'm still junior and still slow on the paperwork the depot wants. I'm also an on-call firefighter in my town, so some nights my pager goes off. I live on my own, I've got about four months of bills saved, and I use AI every day, for routes, fuel costs and working out how to buy my own truck one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, the hype was always bigger than the reality. I'd still say the tools are useful. At the depot I'd tell the lads to use them for the boring stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want my name on the cab door by the time I'm 30, and a quiet AI world is the best chance I'll get. Steady work, steady rates, and I can save for a deposit on my own truck. I'm calm about this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving for the depot and do my class 1 next year. I'd save 300 a month towards a truck deposit. And I'd use AI to compare finance deals and plan the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited about my plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why your own truck?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My granddad had his own lorry, and my dad always said that was the best job he never had. I like being my own boss and I don't mind long hours. The depot even takes owner-drivers on contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money, mostly. Trucks cost a lot and rates are tight. If diesel jumps or the depot cuts rates, I'd wait.

do: Keep driving for the depot and do the **class 1** next year.
Save **300 a month** for a truck deposit.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit excited about my plan.

fieldNote: Ben's dream is being an **owner-driver**, like his grandfather.

Take the class 1 licence next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity for people who learn fast. At the depot I'd show others how to use the apps. Online I'd share tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When an app matches every pallet to the cheapest truck, an owner-driver like me has to be the cheapest or the most reliable, and I can't be the cheapest. The planning and booking side gets automated fast. So my own job's okay, but my dream of being an owner-driver gets harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the freight apps inside out and build a reputation for being reliable. I'd delay buying a truck for a year to watch rates. I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My plan looks shakier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if rates fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. That's the market. If someone does it cheaper, fair enough, I'd have to be better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your firefighting fit in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a bit of extra money and it's my community. I'd keep it no matter what. It also reminds me some jobs need a person on the spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, but complaining won't help. I'd say people need to move quickly. I'd tell the lads to learn new skills now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying my own truck in 2027 would be like buying a horse in 1910. The office side goes in 2028 and the robot trucks around 2031. So my owner-driver plan is dead, and I'd need something else fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the truck plan and keep my savings. I'd look for work where people still need a person, maybe full-time firefighting or a trade. I'd use AI to retrain fast, maybe as an electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but ready to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap between thinking AI and robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me three years to retrain while I still drive. I'd study at night with AI tutors. But I'd be watching rates fall as the planning goes automatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for training. Nobody owes me a living, and I don't want a handout; I want a fair shot at earning one before the robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people to make smart choices. I'd say it calmly and practically. I'd share what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to own one truck and pay it off, but I'd want the loan finished before the robots arrive. Robots around 2034 gives me some time. I'd still be careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a second-hand truck in the first year with a short loan. I'd contract it to the depot and pay it off by 2031. Then I'd sell it and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is buying a truck a smart move with robots coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I pay it off fast and sell it before prices crash. That's the gamble. I'd rather try than wonder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do after selling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe use the money for a trade or a small business. Or join the fire service full time. I'd decide by 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no excuses. I'd tell people to plan like business owners. I'd share my plans online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd want to own the depot, not the truck, because whoever owns the depot owns the loading dock the robots have to use. Robots around 2039 means I'm 40. I think I'd be fine if I plan well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a truck, run it for a few years, then save towards a share in a small depot. I'd learn everything about logistics planning with AI. By 2035 I'd look at buying robot trucks myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Confident, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the big networks squeeze small depots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd team up with other small owners. That's how my granddad did it with his mates. Small people working together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your community fit into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep firefighting, always. It's what keeps me grounded. Robots might drive, but someone still has to run into a burning house.

fieldNote: Ben shifts from owning a truck to owning **infrastructure**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my truck plan dies and I'd have to retrain fast. What would help is short, cheap training courses and fair rules so small firms can compete. Robots might drive, but someone still has to run into a burning house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about community. Small towns need people who stay and help. That matters as much as jobs.

headlineQuote: Nobody owes me a living, and I don't want a handout; I want a fair shot at earning one before the robots do.
portrait: Ben Weber, 27, drives for a **pallet network** depot and is an on-call firefighter.
He uses AI daily and dreams of being an **owner-driver** like his grandfather.
In the fast picture he drops the truck plan and **retrains**, accepting only training help.
With a decade he plans to own part of a **depot** and even robot trucks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which kills his truck plan and forces fast retraining.
whatWouldHelp: Short, cheap **training courses** and fair rules for small firms.
